```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = normalizePath(".."))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7.5, fig.height = 3.8, dpi = 150)
```

```{r load}
source("R/metrics.R")
source("R/imbalance.R")
source("R/plotting.R")
imb <- readRDS("results/imbalance.rds")
tst <- readRDS("results/test.rds")
cv <- readRDS("results/cv.rds")
y_tr <- imb$y
w <- imb$w
f3 <- function(v) sprintf("%.3f", v)
f4 <- function(v) sprintf("%.4f", v)
pct <- function(v, d = 1) sprintf(paste0("%.", d, "f%%"), 100 * v)
```

The numbers on this page come from `scripts/run_test.R`.

## Are the probabilities calibrated?

A model is calibrated if, among the clients it gives a probability $p$, a share
$p$ default. Part 4 turns probabilities into decisions by comparing them with a
cost ratio, so this matters more here than the ranking. Two checks are used: a
reliability diagram, which bins clients by predicted probability, and the
calibration intercept and slope, obtained by regressing the outcome on the
predicted log-odds,

$$
\operatorname{logit} \mathbb{P}(Y = 1 \mid p) = a + b \operatorname{logit}(p).
$$

A calibrated model has $a = 0$ and $b = 1$. A slope below one means the
predictions are too extreme, above one too timid.

```{r calib-table}
cal_row <- function(y, p) {
  cf <- calibration_fit(y, p)
  c(mean_p = mean(p), rate = mean(y), cf)
}
ct <- rbind(
  `Logistic regression` = cal_row(y_tr, tst$oof$logit),
  `XGBoost` = cal_row(y_tr, tst$oof$xgb)
)
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  model = rownames(ct),
  `mean prediction` = pct(ct[, "mean_p"]),
  `default rate` = pct(ct[, "rate"]),
  intercept = sprintf("%+.3f", ct[, "intercept"]),
  slope = f3(ct[, "slope"]),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrr")
```

Both models, fitted without any reweighting, are calibrated out of fold.
No recalibration step (Platt scaling, isotonic regression) is needed, and
adding one would only spend data.

## Rebalancing the classes

`r pct(mean(y_tr))` of the clients default. A common reaction is to rebalance
the training data, either by weighting the defaults by
$w = n_0 / n_1 = `r sprintf("%.2f", w)`$ or by creating synthetic defaults with
SMOTE until the two classes are the same size. Both were tried on the selected
XGBoost configuration, inside the cross-validation folds so that synthetic
clients never reach a validation fold. SMOTE is used in its SMOTE-NC form:
continuous features are interpolated between neighbours, while counts, flags
and months of delay are copied from one of the two clients, since a client
cannot be 2.4 months late.

```{r imb-table}
lab <- c(none = "No rebalancing", weights = "Class weights", smote = "SMOTE-NC")
it <- t(sapply(colnames(imb$oof), function(v) {
  p <- imb$oof[, v]
  c(scores(y_tr, p), mean_p = mean(p), calibration_fit(y_tr, p))
}))
pc <- t(sapply(c("weights", "smote"), function(v) scores(y_tr, prior_correct(imb$oof[, v], w))))
knitr::kable(data.frame(
  training = lab[rownames(it)],
  `mean prediction` = pct(it[, "mean_p"]),
  `log loss` = f4(it[, "log_loss"]),
  AUC = f3(it[, "auc"]),
  `calibration intercept` = sprintf("%+.2f", it[, "intercept"]),
  `log loss after correction` = c("", f4(pc[, "log_loss"])),
  check.names = FALSE
), row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrr")
```

Rebalancing does not help the model tell good and bad clients apart: class
weights leave the AUC unchanged and SMOTE lowers it. What it does is move every
probability up. With class weights the mean prediction is
`r pct(it["weights", "mean_p"])` for a default rate of `r pct(mean(y_tr))`,
and the log loss is as bad as that of the constant model
(`r f4(log_loss(y_tr, rep(mean(y_tr), length(y_tr))))`).

The shift is predictable. Weighting the defaults by $w$ multiplies the odds the
model estimates by $w$, so the original probabilities are recovered by

$$
\tilde p = \frac{p}{p + w (1 - p)}.
$$

After this correction the weighted model is as good as the unweighted one: the
whole effect of the weights was a change of scale. The same correction does not
fully repair SMOTE, whose synthetic clients are not draws from the population of
defaulters, and SMOTE stays worse on every measure.

```{r reliability, fig.height = 3.8}
rel <- function(y, p, panel, curve) cbind(reliability(y, p), panel = panel, curve = curve)
d <- rbind(
  rel(y_tr, tst$oof$logit, "Selected models", "Logistic regression"),
  rel(y_tr, tst$oof$xgb, "Selected models", "XGBoost"),
  rel(y_tr, imb$oof[, "weights"], "XGBoost with rebalancing", "Class weights"),
  rel(y_tr, imb$oof[, "smote"], "XGBoost with rebalancing", "SMOTE-NC"),
  rel(y_tr, prior_correct(imb$oof[, "weights"], w), "XGBoost with rebalancing", "Class weights, corrected")
)
d$curve <- factor(d$curve, levels = c("Logistic regression", "XGBoost", "Class weights",
                                      "SMOTE-NC", "Class weights, corrected"))
ggplot(d, aes(predicted, observed, colour = curve)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey70", linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  facet_wrap(~panel) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = unname(c(palette_main[c("accent", "dark")], "#d08c3c", "#7f6aa8", palette_main["mid"]))) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_axis, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_axis, limits = c(0, 1)) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(title = "Reliability on the training set, out of fold",
       subtitle = "Clients grouped in deciles of predicted probability",
       x = "Mean predicted probability", y = "Observed default rate") +
  theme_report() +
  theme(legend.position = "right", panel.spacing = unit(1.5, "lines")) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 1))
```

The practical consequence is that rebalancing and the choice of a decision
threshold do the same job. A model trained with weights $w$ and cut at 0.5
flags, up to estimation noise, the same clients as the unweighted model cut at
$1 / (1 + w)$. Doing both,
as in the original version of this project (SMOTE, then a threshold tuned on
balanced accuracy), corrects for the imbalance twice. The models below are
trained on the data as it is, and the threshold is set in part 4 from the costs.

## Test set

The two selected models were refitted on the whole training set with the
hyperparameters chosen in part 2 and scored once on the
`r format(length(tst$y), big.mark = ",")` test clients. Nothing on the previous
pages was changed after this.

```{r test-table}
yt <- tst$y
Lt <- sapply(tst$pred, function(p) -(yt * log(p) + (1 - yt) * log(1 - p)))
set.seed(2)
idx <- replicate(2000, sample.int(length(yt), replace = TRUE))
boot_ci <- function(stat) {
  q <- quantile(apply(idx, 2, stat), c(0.025, 0.975))
  sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", q[1], q[2])
}
tl <- c(constant = "Constant", rule = "Rule PAY_1 >= 2", logit = "Logistic regression", xgb = "XGBoost")
tt <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(tl), function(m) {
  p <- tst$pred[[m]]
  data.frame(
    model = tl[m],
    `log loss` = f4(log_loss(yt, p)),
    `95% interval` = boot_ci(function(i) mean(Lt[i, m])),
    Brier = f4(brier(yt, p)),
    AUC = if (m == "constant") "0.500" else f3(auc(yt, p)),
    `AUC 95% interval` = if (m == "constant") "" else boot_ci(function(i) auc(yt[i], p[i])),
    check.names = FALSE
  )
}))
knitr::kable(tt, row.names = FALSE, align = "lrrrrr")
dxl <- Lt[, "xgb"] - Lt[, "logit"]
dxr <- Lt[, "xgb"] - Lt[, "rule"]
q_xl <- quantile(apply(idx, 2, function(i) mean(dxl[i])), c(0.025, 0.975))
q_xr <- quantile(apply(idx, 2, function(i) mean(dxr[i])), c(0.025, 0.975))
cal_t <- rbind(logit = calibration_fit(yt, tst$pred$logit), xgb = calibration_fit(yt, tst$pred$xgb))
cv_xgb <- log_loss(y_tr, tst$oof$xgb)
```

The ranking of part 2 holds on new clients. XGBoost beats the logistic
regression by `r f4(-mean(dxl))` in log loss (paired 95% interval
`r sprintf("[%.4f, %.4f]", -q_xl[2], -q_xl[1])`) and the rule by
`r f4(-mean(dxr))` (`r sprintf("[%.4f, %.4f]", -q_xr[2], -q_xr[1])`). Its test log
loss is `r f4(log_loss(yt, tst$pred$xgb))`, against `r f4(cv_xgb)` out of fold:
the gap is the optimism left by tuning on the training folds, plus sampling
noise, and it is small.

Calibration also carries over. On the test set the calibration slope is
`r f3(cal_t["xgb", "slope"])` for XGBoost and `r f3(cal_t["logit", "slope"])`
for the logistic regression, with intercepts of
`r sprintf("%+.3f", cal_t["xgb", "intercept"])` and
`r sprintf("%+.3f", cal_t["logit", "intercept"])`.

For comparison, the original version of this project reported an AUC of 0.772
for XGBoost, on a single split with no tuning and different features. The
difference with the AUC above is within the sampling noise of a 7,500-client
test set, which is why the comparisons on this page are paired and why part 5
repeats the procedure over several splits.
